ChromaDB/similarity_search.py.purpose: Creates a small in-memory ChromaDB collection of 14 grocery items, then asks for the three items whose meaning is closest to the word "apple". This is the smallest complete example of a vector database in the whole repository: create, fill, query, read.
ChromaDB/similarity_search.py.run: python similarity_search.py   (run from inside the ChromaDB folder)
meta: downloads the MiniLM model on first run

sections.title: Imports and the embedding model
sections.why: Before you can store text in a vector database, some model has to convert text into numbers. ChromaDB ships a wrapper that does exactly that.

sections.title: Client, collection name and the empty main() stub
sections.why: The client is the connection to the database. Here it is in-memory, like writing on a whiteboard instead of a register - everything is gone when the program ends.

sections.title: Delete-then-create: start from a clean slate
sections.why: Running a demo twice should give the same answer. Deleting first removes yesterday's data, so duplicates can never pile up.

sections.title: The grocery catalogue (14 short texts)
sections.why: These are the "documents". For ChromaDB a document is just a string; meaning is added later by the embedding model.

sections.title: Unique IDs and ingestion
sections.why: Every stored vector needs a name. IDs must be unique strings, otherwise ChromaDB refuses the insert.

sections.title: Reading data back
sections.why: A quick sanity check that the insert really happened before trusting the search.

sections.title: The similarity search function
sections.why: This is the heart of retrieval: embed the query with the same model, compare against every stored vector, keep the closest few.

sections.title: Run it
sections.why: The last line actually starts the demo. Everything above only defined things.

notes.title: Why a second import?
notes.text: `chromadb` is the database itself; `embedding_functions` is the toolbox of ready-made text-to-number converters. Keeping them separate means you can swap the model without touching the database code.

notes.title: The embedding function: your text-to-numbers machine
notes.text: `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is a small open model that turns any sentence into 384 numbers. Think of it as a clerk who reads every dish and writes 384 ratings for it (how sweet, how fruity, how savoury...). Similar dishes get similar ratings. It downloads once (~90 MB) and then runs on your CPU, so no internet and no API key are needed later.

notes.title: In-memory client
notes.text: `chromadb.Client()` keeps everything in RAM. Close the program and the collection disappears. For homework demos that is a feature, not a bug: you never leave half-broken data behind. In a real product you would use `chromadb.PersistentClient(path=...)`.

notes.title: One string, used everywhere
notes.text: Two other lines refer to this same name (delete and create). Keeping it in a variable means you cannot accidentally delete one collection and create another with a slightly different spelling.

notes.title: A stub that does nothing
notes.text: `main()` only contains `pass` inside a `try`. It is a placeholder the course leaves for you. Note that it is never called anywhere in this file, so it has zero effect. Its `except Exception as error` is a reminder of the pattern used at the bottom of the file: catch broadly, print, move on.

notes.title: Destructive on purpose
notes.text: This deletes the collection if it exists. There is no `try`/`except` around it, so on a *truly* fresh client ChromaDB may raise an error saying the collection does not exist. If you hit that, wrap it the way `_walkthrough`'s sibling project (Food_Recommender) does: `try: client.delete_collection(...) except: pass`.

notes.title: Create the collection, with its rules
notes.text: Three things are decided here: the **name**, some **metadata** (a description and the distance metric), and the **embedding function** that will be used for every insert and every query. Binding the model to the collection is what guarantees that documents and queries are converted the same way.

notes.title: The measuring tape: cosine distance
notes.text: `hnsw:space` picks how "closeness" is measured. `cosine` compares the *direction* of two vectors and ignores their length, which is exactly what you want for text. Distance 0 = same direction (very similar), 2 = opposite. With 14 grocery items, the top matches usually sit between 0 and 1.

notes.title: The mini catalogue
notes.text: Fourteen phrases, some deliberately tricky: "fresh red apples", "golden apple" and "red fruit" are near-duplicates in meaning, while "whole wheat bread" is a different kind of food. A good search should rank all three apple-ish rows above the bread, even though only one of them contains the exact word "apple".

notes.title: List comprehension for IDs
notes.text: `enumerate` gives `(0, text), (1, text), ...`. The `_` says "I do not need this value". Adding 1 turns 0-based indexes into human-friendly IDs: `food_1` ... `food_14`. ChromaDB requires strings, and an f-string guarantees that.

notes.title: Insert documents, metadata and IDs together
notes.text: Three parallel lists: `documents[i]` is the text, `metadatas[i]` is extra searchable/filterable data about it, `ids[i]` is its name. ChromaDB embeds each document with `ef` automatically - you never call `encode()` yourself. The metadata list is built with a comprehension so every row gets the same two tags.

notes.title: Metadata = the label on the jar
notes.text: Metadata values must be simple (string, number, boolean) - never lists or `None`. Here every item is tagged `food`. In a bigger app you would store `calories`, `cuisine`, `price` here and then filter on them during search, exactly like the Food_Recommender tab does.

notes.title: Read without any similarity maths
notes.text: `get()` returns everything stored. It is the equivalent of `SELECT *` and is useful for debugging: if this prints 14, your ingestion worked and any later problem is in the query path, not the data path.

notes.title: The cheapest test you can write
notes.text: One number tells you whether the insert succeeded. Beginners often skip this and then spend an hour debugging a "bad search" that is really an empty database.

notes.title: One function, one job
notes.text: It takes the collection and an object it never actually uses (`all_items` is passed but ignored). That is harmless here, but it is a good habit to notice: unused parameters make readers hunt for a hidden dependency that does not exist.

notes.title: One word is enough
notes.text: The query is plain text, not a vector. The collection's embedding function converts it behind the scenes, using the same model that embedded the 14 items - the single most important rule of vector search.

notes.title: The actual search call
notes.text: `query_texts=[...]` is a list because you may ask several questions at once. `n_results=3` says "give me the three nearest neighbours". Under the hood ChromaDB compares the query vector against all 14 stored vectors using cosine distance and sorts them.

notes.at: if not results or not results['ids'] or len(results['ids'][0]) == 0:
notes.title: Always guard a search result
notes.text: ChromaDB wraps answers in a list-per-query, so `results['ids'][0]` is the answer to the first (only) query. If the collection is empty this is an empty list, and indexing it blindly would crash. This guard prints a friendly message and returns early.

notes.title: Why min(3, ...)?
notes.text: You asked for 3, but a tiny collection might return fewer. `min` takes whatever is smaller, so the loop can never ask for a row that does not exist.

notes.title: Distance, not percentage
notes.text: This is a **distance**: smaller is better, 0 means identical. Do not print it as a match percentage. Convert with `1 - distance` first if you want a similarity score the way Food_Recommender does.

notes.title: Defensive text printing
notes.text: ChromaDB can technically return an empty document. The `if not text` branch prints "Text not available" so the output stays neat instead of showing `None`. `{score:.4f}` rounds to four decimals to keep columns aligned.

notes.title: Catch-all at the boundary
notes.text: A one-line script should not dump a traceback at a learner. Catching `Exception` here keeps the console readable. In production code you would log the traceback instead of hiding it.
